title: Nothing on our own
hookLine: on our own we can do nothing; all happens in His color (Sukhmani 15)

lines: THE COLOR GOES INTO EVERY THREAD.
cards: In old Punjab, cloth was dyed by hand. You'd soak plain white cotton in a vat, and when you lifted it out, it had become saffron, or indigo, or deep red. A good dye doesn't sit on top of the cloth like paint.
It goes into every thread. You can't scrape it off. The cloth is still cloth, but every part of it carries the color.
Gurbani returns to that picture, and today it's the way into a hard teaching: nothing on our own.

teach.h: THE DOER OF ALL, ANOTHER SIDE.
teach.b: Back in the eleventh ashtpadi, Sukhmani called God the doer of all. The fifteenth comes at that thought from another side.
Its first stanza says, in paraphrase: nothing happens by a person's own doing, though they long for it a hundred times. Gurbani elsewhere gives that thought a color.
Rang means color and dye, but in Punjabi it also means joy, love, mood, the delight of a festival. So being dyed in His rang says more than: God controls everything.
It pictures everything soaked in God, the way dyed cloth is soaked in color.
Our actions are still ours, the way the cloth is still cloth. Sikhs work hard, study, serve and plan; nobody is told to sit and wait.
But in this picture every thread of that doing is already colored by the One Sukhmani calls the Giver, the One full of every power.
The strength in the arms, the idea that arrived, the breath that let the sentence finish: none of it, the stanza says, comes by our own doing alone.
One version of this picture in Gurbani is a deep red dye from the madder root, majeeth.

Cloth dyed with majeeth was said to keep its color through every wash, and hymns ask to be dyed like that, so deeply in the Name that nothing washes it out. So nothing on our own isn't an insult to your effort.
It's a description of what your effort is made of.
And when the doing is soaked in someone else's color, the natural response, once it's done, is thanks.

how: Gurbani often speaks of being dyed in the Name, like cloth in fast madder dye, and Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's fifteenth ashtpadi hear that nothing is done by one's own doing alone.

o: color and dye, and also joy and love
a caste or class a person is born into
the outward look of a person's clothes

games.q: nothing on our own — tap the pairs.
p: madder: the red dye that stays

s: nothing on our own means Sikhs should sit and wait
Sikhs work, study, serve and plan; the doing is just soaked in God's color.
rang in Punjabi can mean color and also joy or love
everything happening in His rang is soaked in God, like dye.
majeeth, in Gurbani, is a dye that washes out easily
majeeth, madder, was said to keep its color through every wash.

games.q: you just finished a hard project and it went well. by the fifteenth ashtpadi, what's the natural next move?
o: take full credit; you did it.
give thanks; the doing was soaked in His color.
pretend you didn't really do anything.
games.why: thanks. the effort was really yours, like cloth is really cloth, but every thread carried the color of the Giver.

practice: Pick something tiny you can do right here, straighten your back, take one slow, full breath, unclench your hands, and do it with attention.

Then notice what made it possible, the muscles, the air, the moment of quiet, and let a thank-you rise to whoever or whatever you understand that to be. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each thank-you.

wordCard.voice: Rang, color, dye, also joy. Nothing comes by our own doing alone; in Gurbani's picture it is soaked in His rang, like cloth soaked through with dye.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rang, color or dye, and also joy, love or delight.

carryVoice: Your line: in his color. Still cloth, soaked through. Four hundred ninety-six days, and counting.
